situation.person: Mother or primary caregiver of a newborn (0-3 weeks), in Nigeria/Africa or the diaspora, responsible for daily umbilical stump care - often with conflicting advice from grandmothers, aunties and hospital staff about what to apply and what to avoid
situation.specific_situation: The baby's umbilical stump is still attached and must be kept clean and dry while relatives insist on traditional substances (toothpaste, shea butter, herbs, hot compresses) and hospital discharge instructions said something different
situation.timeframe: Birth to cord separation (typically 5-15 days; up to 3 weeks normal)
situation.trigger: Hospital discharge with vague cord instructions plus immediate arrival of family helpers with strong opinions
situation.problem: She does not know which daily care routine is actually safe, which traditional practices are harmless versus dangerous, and which changes in the stump's appearance mean 'normal healing' versus 'infection needing a doctor tonight'
situation.failed_attempt: Tried following the grandmother's advice (e.g. applying toothpaste or tying a belly band) while secretly worrying; or cleaned with everything the pharmacy suggested because no one gave one clear routine
constraints: Conflicting authority figures in the home
No pediatrician appointment until weeks later
Fear that questioning elders causes conflict
Limited access to same-day medical advice
situation.emotional_stake: She believes her baby could die from a cord infection she failed to prevent, and fears being blamed by the family if anything goes wrong either way
situation.desired_transformation: One clear, evidence-based daily routine; confidence to protect the stump from harmful substances without family war; and the exact red flags that mean seek care immediately

current_behavior: Applying whatever substance the most senior relative recommends
Cleaning the stump with multiple antiseptics
Covering the stump with belly bands or coins
current_conditions: Substances applied on top of hospital instructions
No agreed household rule for who decides cord questions
emotional_state: Guilt and fear about causing infection
practical_consequences: Infection signs missed or over-reacted to
failed_attempts: Toothpaste, shea butter, methylated spirit layered together
Asking three different people and getting three answers
environmental_constraints: Home birth or early discharge common
Chlorhexidine gel not stocked in many pharmacies

new_capabilities: Can name which traditional substances are dangerous vs unnecessary
Runs a daily 30-second check with clear pass/fail criteria
improvements: Family conflict reduced by pre-agreed rules
systems_created: A written cord-care house rule everyone in the home follows
remaining_limits: Does not replace newborn wellness visits
evidence_of_change: Zero harmful substances applied after starting
Caregiver can state the five red flags unprompted
Timely clinic presentation when flags appear

mechanism.core_mechanism: Replace conflicting folklore with ONE default (clean, dry, exposed) plus a decision tree that converts anxiety into observable criteria, and scripts that de-escalate family pressure without confrontation
mechanisms: Default-action design removes daily judgement (the routine never asks opinion)
Red-flag card converts diffuse fear into five observable signs mapped to action levels
Respect-scripts give the mother words that honour elders while protecting the baby
mechanism.why_it_should_work: WHO and AAP guidance show dry cord care is safe and effective where hygiene allows; most harm comes from applied substances and moisture, so removing decisions and substances removes the risk pathway

evidence_basis.claim: Clean, dry cord care is WHO's recommendation for facility births and low neonatal-mortality settings
evidence_basis.source: WHO recommendations on postnatal care of the mother and newborn (2014); WHO 2022 positive postnatal experience guideline

evidence_basis.claim: Daily 7.1% chlorhexidine application is recommended only for HOME births in high neonatal-mortality settings (>30/1000), or to replace harmful traditional substances
evidence_basis.source: WHO postnatal care recommendations (2014); Healthy Newborn Network Country Guidance (2015/2018)

evidence_basis.claim: Umbilical stump normally separates within roughly 5-15 days; separation after 3 weeks warrants medical review
evidence_basis.source: American Academy of Pediatrics, Pediatrics 2016;138(3):e20162149; Cleveland Clinic omphalitis guidance (2024)

evidence_basis.claim: Methylated spirit was non-inferior to 4% chlorhexidine gel for preventing omphalitis in a randomized trial in Jos, Nigeria (323 mother-baby pairs)
evidence_basis.source: Shwe DD et al., Nigerian Journal of Clinical Practice 2021;24(5) (PMID 34018987)

evidence_basis.claim: Common applied substances in Nigerian practice include toothpaste (8.9%) and hot compresses (24.8%); hot compresses and herbal pastes are the documented dangers, not spirit alone
evidence_basis.source: Onubogu CU et al., Asian Journal of Pediatric Research 2022;8(2):1-10 (Nnewi survey)

evidence_basis.claim: Omphalitis red flags are spreading periumbilical redness, purulent/foul discharge, swelling/hardening, fever >=38C or temperature instability, poor feeding/lethargy; any sign needs same-day medical care
Omphalitis can progress to sepsis rapidly; newborns may show hypothermia instead of fever

transformation_path.objective: Establish the baseline: what is currently being applied, by whom, and why
Install ONE written household cord rule before opinions arrive
customer_action: Send the announcement script to key relatives

transformation_path.objective: Execute clean-dry-exposed care with a 30-second daily check

transformation_path.stage: Decide fast when something looks wrong
transformation_path.objective: Convert worry into triage using observable criteria
customer_action: Run the decision tree at every change

transformation_path.objective: Handle separation event, granuloma awareness, delayed separation

failure_point_map.scenario: Grandmother applies toothpaste/sheabutter during a nap
failure_point_map.rescue_protocol: Do-not-blame reset script: clean gently with water, restate house rule, move stump-supplies out of reach; log the incident, watch 48h extra

failure_point_map.failure_type: stump looks 'wrong' but baby is well
failure_point_map.scenario: Yellowish crusting or mild smell causes panic at midnight
failure_point_map.rescue_protocol: Decision tree normal/worry branches; if no red flags, continue routine and re-check in 12h; document photo for clinic

failure_point_map.scenario: Spreading redness, pus, fever >=38C or lethargy
failure_point_map.rescue_protocol: Rescue card: same-day medical care - emergency numbers per region; do not apply anything else to the stump
Book medical review; note whether dry or moist; no pulling, twisting, or home removal attempts

failure_point_map.scenario: New helper arrives week two with fresh advice
failure_point_map.rescue_protocol: Handover card: new helper reads the one-page house rule before touching baby care duties

first_win.action: Write the House Rule ('Nothing goes on the stump. Clean, dry, exposed.') on the fridge card and send the respect-script message to the two most influential relatives
first_win.observable_change: A posted rule exists and the household's next response to advice is the script, not an argument

before_baseline: Number of substances applied to stump in last 48h
Household disagreement events about cord care
success_indicators: Zero harmful substances applied from Day 1 to separation
All red-flag events resulted in same-day care
Zero major family conflicts over cord care
tsm.success_threshold: 60%+ of completers meet >=3 of 4 indicators at Day 30 review
tsm.measurement_method: Self-reported daily log + structured Day-30 check-in against baseline
tsm.incomplete_progress_interpretation: Partial adherence is expected during family pressure spikes; only harmful-substance exposure resets progress to Day 1 of run phase
tsm.next_action_on_miss: Re-run the Diagnose stage with the specific person who applied substances; install handover card for helpers

maintenance.maintenance_system: After separation: weekly navel check inside bath routine until fully healed
maintenance.relapse_protocol: If any substance is applied again post-separation due to rash/bleeding worries: stop, photograph, route through decision tree rather than home treatment
maintenance.reentry_protocol: Restart at Stage 3 (routine) with whoever now performs baby care; no guilt reset

evidence.claim: Dry cord care standard for facility births
CHX indication limited to high-mortality home-birth settings or replacing harmful substances
Nigerian practice prevalence data (spirit 89%, hot compress 25%, toothpaste 9%)
Jos RCT non-inferiority of methylated spirit
Omphalitis red-flag set and sepsis progression risk

safety.scope_boundary: This system coordinates everyday cord hygiene and triage ONLY. It never diagnoses infection, never treats with antibiotics, never advises removing the stump, and never replaces newborn wellness visits. Any suspected infection routes to professional care.
red_flags: Redness spreading outward from the stump base onto the belly skin
Pus (yellow/green/white thick fluid) or foul smell
Swelling or hardening of skin around the stump
Fever >=38C rectal OR abnormally low temperature OR baby feels hot/cold to touch
Poor feeding, unusual sleepiness, difficulty waking, inconsolable crying
Active bleeding that does not stop with 10 minutes of gentle pressure
escalation_rules: Any single red flag = same-day medical care; fever or lethargy = emergency now
Use verified local emergency/paediatric contacts from the shared crisis-escalation list
When unsure, present to care - newborns deteriorate fast and 'wait-and-see' is never the instruction

research_disposition.rationale: Flagship #2 from naming audit (score 86). Distinct situation (daily cord decisions under family pressure) + distinct transformation (safe default routine + triage competence).
